specPoints.text: understand how metals can be arranged in a reactivity series based on their displacement reactions between: metals and metal oxides; metals and aqueous solutions of metal salts

primer.text: From Metals Reacting with Water & Acids you have seen how vigour with water and acids ranks the metals. This note adds the second ranking tool: displacement. A more reactive metal takes a less reactive metal's place in its oxide or in its salt solution, and deciding which displacements succeed orders any pair of metals without needing water at all.

lessons.title: Metal displacement reactions
lessons.opening: Reactivity falls going down the series, so the stronger metal pushes a weaker one out of its compounds. Two routes show this: heating a metal together with a metal oxide, and standing a metal in the watery solution of another metal's compound. Heating copper(II) oxide with zinc, for example, leaves the zinc holding the oxygen, and the zinc is the reducing agent in the reaction.
keyPoints: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compounds.
One route heats a metal together with a metal oxide.
Zinc reduces copper(II) oxide on heating: Zn + CuO gives ZnO + Cu.
The reducing agent in that reaction is the zinc, which takes the oxygen for itself.
Sodium oxide and magnesium show no reaction, because sodium already outranks magnesium.

low.restatement: Put a hungrier metal next to a compound of a calmer one and the hungry metal takes its place. Heat zinc with copper(II) oxide and the zinc grabs the oxygen, leaving copper metal behind, because zinc sits above copper on the ladder.
low.analogy: Like a stronger player taking a seat at a board game: the swap only works when the newcomer outranks the one sitting down, and the loser leaves empty-handed.
low.examPointer: Name which metal ends up as the oxide and which as the metal, and point out the reducing agent; the displacement direction is where the mark sits.

medium.restatement: In oxide displacement the more reactive metal removes the oxygen from the less reactive metal's oxide, acting as the reducing agent while the oxide is reduced. The thermite reaction of iron(III) oxide with aluminium is the extreme case, and pairings that run the wrong way, like sodium oxide with magnesium, show no reaction.
medium.analogy: Think of oxygen as a prize that only the more eager metal can snatch: whoever grips it harder walks away with the oxide, and the loser walks away as the bare metal.
medium.examPointer: Practise reading the oxide table both ways: predicting products for a reactive pair and predicting no reaction for an uphill pair.

check.stem: When zinc is heated with copper(II) oxide, which metal ends up as the oxide?

options.text: Zinc, because it is the more reactive metal and takes the oxygen
options.explanation: Zinc outranks copper, so it pulls the oxygen away and leaves copper metal behind.

options.text: Copper, because the oxide never changes
options.explanation: The whole point of the displacement is that the oxide transfers to the more reactive metal.

options.text: Neither, both metals stay as they started
options.explanation: The reaction visibly proceeds: zinc becomes zinc oxide and copper appears as metal.

options.text: Both share the oxygen equally
options.explanation: Displacement is a clean takeover; the oxygen ends with the more reactive metal alone.

check.stem: In the reaction Zn + CuO → ZnO + Cu, what is the role of the zinc?

options.text: It is the reducing agent, removing oxygen from the copper(II) oxide
options.explanation: The zinc takes the oxygen for itself, which reduces the copper compound and oxidises the zinc.

options.text: It is the catalyst, speeding the reaction without changing
options.explanation: The zinc is consumed, becoming zinc oxide; a catalyst would emerge unchanged.

options.text: It is the oxidising agent, giving oxygen away
options.explanation: Zinc receives oxygen rather than giving it; the oxide is what supplies the oxygen.

options.text: It has no special role beyond filling space
options.explanation: The zinc is the active partner; its reactivity is what drives the whole displacement.

check.stem: Why does a mixture of sodium oxide and magnesium show no reaction on heating?

options.text: Because sodium is above magnesium in the series, so magnesium cannot displace it
options.explanation: Displacement runs only downhill; magnesium is the less reactive metal and cannot take sodium's oxygen.

options.text: Because the temperature is never high enough for any displacement
options.explanation: Heat is sufficient for reactive pairs; the block here is the order of reactivity, not the temperature.

options.text: Because sodium oxide is insoluble
options.explanation: Solubility is irrelevant to the oxide route; the series order alone decides the outcome.

options.text: Because both metals are unreactive
options.explanation: Sodium is among the most reactive metals; the mixture is quiet precisely because magnesium is the weaker partner.

check.stem: The thermite reaction uses iron(III) oxide and aluminium. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text: Aluminium displaces iron, giving iron metal and aluminium oxide
options.explanation: Aluminium sits above iron, so it takes the oxygen and the iron is freed, matching Fe2O3 + 2Al giving 2Fe + Al2O3.

options.text: Iron displaces aluminium, giving aluminium metal and iron oxide
options.explanation: That runs uphill; iron sits below aluminium and cannot take its oxygen.

options.text: No reaction occurs because both are metals
options.explanation: Metal-versus-metal-oxide is exactly the setup where the more reactive metal wins the oxygen.

options.text: The products are iron sulfide and aluminium
options.explanation: No sulfur is present; the products are iron and aluminium oxide.

check.stem: Lead(II) oxide is heated with silver. What happens, given lead is more reactive than silver?

options.text: No reaction, because silver cannot displace the more reactive lead from its oxide
options.explanation: The mixture runs uphill, so the silver stays silver and the lead(II) oxide stays intact.

options.text: Silver takes the oxygen, giving silver oxide and lead
options.explanation: That requires silver to outrank lead, which is the reverse of the truth.

options.text: The two metals swap places halfway
options.explanation: Displacement is all-or-nothing by the series order; there is no partial swap.

options.text: The lead metal appears and the oxide vanishes
options.explanation: That would need silver to be the reducing agent, which it cannot be here.

lessons.title: Displacement reactions between metals & aqueous solutions of metal salts
sourceHeadings: Displacement reactions between metals & aqueous solutions of metal salts
lessons.opening: The second displacement route compares two metals in salt solutions: a strip of one metal goes into an aqueous solution of another metal's salt. If the strip's metal is the more reactive, it slowly disappears into the solution, displacing the less reactive metal, which appears as solid. Magnesium in copper(II) sulfate shows it beautifully, as the blue colour fades while copper coats the magnesium.
keyPoints: A metal strip placed in an aqueous solution of another metal's salt can displace it.
The stronger metal gradually fades into the solution while the weaker one appears as solid.
Magnesium in copper(II) sulfate gives MgSO4 and copper: Mg + CuSO4 gives MgSO4 + Cu.
The blue colour of the copper(II) sulfate fades as colourless magnesium sulfate forms.
Copper coats the magnesium surface and also falls to the bottom as solid metal.

low.restatement: Stand one metal in a solution of another metal's salt: if the standing metal is more reactive, it swaps places with the dissolved one. The blue copper(II) sulfate fades as magnesium takes copper's seat and copper metal appears.
low.analogy: Like a queue where someone further forward can send someone behind them back: the swap happens one way only, and you can see the colour change as it does.
low.examPointer: Describe the fading blue colour and the copper deposit together; both are the standard observations for this reaction.

medium.restatement: In salt-solution displacement the more reactive metal's atoms enter the solution as ions while the dissolved metal's ions leave as solid, so the strip visibly corrodes as the other metal deposits. The colour change tracks the swap: copper(II) sulfate's blue fades as magnesium sulfate forms, and pairings that run uphill, such as zinc in sodium chloride, show no reaction.
medium.analogy: Picture a musical-chairs game between atoms and ions: the more reactive atom always wins the seat in solution, and the loser is left standing as solid metal.
medium.examPointer: Use the solutions table to predict outcomes quickly: downhill pairings react with a colour change, uphill pairings show nothing.

check.stem: What is seen when a piece of magnesium is left in blue copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.text: The blue colour fades and copper coats the magnesium
options.explanation: Magnesium displaces copper, forming colourless magnesium sulfate while copper deposits on the strip and at the bottom.

options.text: The blue colour deepens as more copper forms
options.explanation: The blue belongs to dissolved copper(II); as it leaves the solution the colour fades, not deepens.

options.text: Nothing happens, because magnesium is unreactive
options.explanation: Magnesium is well above copper, so the displacement proceeds readily.

options.text: The solution turns orange as bromine forms
options.explanation: No halogen is present; orange belongs to bromine chemistry, not to this metal displacement.

check.stem: Which equation represents magnesium displacing copper from copper(II) sulfate?

options.text: Mg + CuSO4 gives MgSO4 + Cu
options.explanation: The metals simply swap partners with the sulfate, and every atom count balances one-for-one.

options.text: Mg + CuSO4 gives MgCu + SO4
options.explanation: The sulfate stays with a metal; it does not float free, and no MgCu compound exists here.

options.text: Mg + CuSO4 gives MgO + CuS
options.explanation: Neither oxygen nor sulfur is freed in this swap; the sulfate group stays intact with the magnesium.

options.text: 2Mg + CuSO4 gives 2MgSO4 + Cu
options.explanation: The magnesiums do not balance: two in, but only one sulfate to pair with each.

check.stem: Why does zinc show no reaction in sodium chloride solution?

options.text: Because sodium is above zinc in the reactivity series
options.explanation: Zinc cannot displace a metal that outranks it, so the solution stays unchanged.

options.text: Because sodium chloride is not a salt
options.explanation: Sodium chloride is a perfectly ordinary salt; the quiet comes from the series order.

options.text: Because zinc is too reactive to enter the solution
options.explanation: Reactivity is what drives displacement, not what blocks it; zinc simply lacks the rank here.

options.text: Because chlorine gas forms a protective layer
options.explanation: No chlorine gas is involved; the salt's chloride stays dissolved throughout.

check.stem: Lead is placed in silver nitrate solution. What are the products, given lead outranks silver?

options.text: Lead(II) nitrate and silver metal
options.explanation: Lead takes the nitrate's company and silver is displaced as solid, matching Pb + 2AgNO3 giving Pb(NO3)2 + 2Ag.

options.text: Silver nitrate and lead metal
options.explanation: That is the starting set; the displacement moves lead into the solution and brings silver out.

options.text: Lead oxide and silver nitrate
options.explanation: No oxygen is freed in salt-solution displacement; the nitrate stays whole.

options.text: No reaction occurs
options.explanation: Lead sits above silver, so the displacement runs downhill and does proceed.

check.stem: How do displacement reactions arrange metals in a reactivity series?

options.text: Each successful displacement shows the added metal is more reactive, so the outcomes order any pair tested
options.explanation: Downhill displacements succeed and uphill ones fail, which is exactly the evidence the series is built from.

options.text: By weighing how much of each metal dissolves
options.explanation: The ranking comes from which displacements succeed, not from measured masses.

options.text: By the colours of the salts alone
options.explanation: Colours help identify products, but the ranking evidence is which swaps happen.

options.text: Displacement reactions cannot order metals at all
options.explanation: Both displacement routes, oxides and salt solutions, are precisely the tools the specification names for this ranking.

glossary.definition: A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive one in its compound.
The substance that removes oxygen from another in a reaction, here the more reactive metal.
A substance dissolved in water, such as the metal salt solutions used in displacement tests.
The highly exothermic displacement in which aluminium takes oxygen from iron(III) oxide.
An ionic compound of a metal with a non-metal group, such as copper(II) sulfate or sodium chloride.

workedExample.prompt: Predict the outcome of each and write the equation where one exists: a) zinc heated with copper(II) oxide; b) a magnesium strip left in copper(II) sulfate solution; c) a zinc strip left in sodium chloride solution. d) State the role of zinc in reaction (a).
steps: a) Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the oxide: Zn + CuO → ZnO + Cu.
b) Magnesium is more reactive than copper: Mg + CuSO4 → MgSO4 + Cu — the blue colour fades as colourless magnesium sulfate forms and brown copper coats the magnesium.
c) No reaction: sodium sits above zinc in the reactivity series, so zinc cannot displace it from its salt.
d) Zinc takes the oxygen from copper(II) oxide for itself, so zinc is the reducing agent.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Zn + CuO → ZnO + Cu. b) Mg + CuSO4 → MgSO4 + Cu (blue fades, copper deposits). c) No reaction. d) Zinc is the reducing agent.
